analysis.one_liner: Exempts federal-land oil and gas drilling from state environmental laws and eases federal permitting.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 18 cosponsors, all Republicans, the bill was referred to two House committees and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have exempted oil and gas drilling on federal lands, including offshore submerged lands, from state environmental and pollution control laws. It would have required federal agencies to issue drilling permits within 60 days of a single consolidated environmental review, sharply limited the Interior Department's power to suspend leases, made suspensions exceeding 90 days a taxpayer liability, funneled all appeals through the D.C. Court of Appeals with tight deadlines, and imposed attorney fees on citizens and groups who sued drillers and lost. The bill was introduced with 18 cosponsors, referred to two House committees, and never received a vote before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, companies holding federal and offshore oil and gas leases would have gained the most: they would have been exempt from state environmental and pollution control laws, could have gotten permits through a single environmental review with a 60-day mandatory deadline, could only have had their leases suspended in narrow emergencies, would have been entitled to taxpayer-paid damages if a suspension lasted too long, and would have been shielded by new fee penalties against people who sued them and lost.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas companies leasing federal land

how_it_helps.text: For the oil and gas companies it serves, the bill would have wiped out state environmental and pollution control laws on any activity under a federal lease, including offshore submerged lands.

It would have replaced separate environmental reviews for each plan and permit with a single statement and single review covering everything under the lease, with a mandate that every federal permitting official issue the permit within 60 days.

It would have stopped the Interior Secretary from suspending a lease unless there was clear proof of an imminent threat to public safety or significant damage, and made suspensions lasting more than 90 days in six months a breach of contract entitling the company to damages or a refund of its bonus bid.

It would have moved all appeals to the D.C. Court of Appeals, defaulted to the lessee if the government missed a deadline, and made losing plaintiffs liable for the drillers' attorney fees, witness fees, and court costs, including third parties who funded indigent plaintiffs.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, state governments would have lost their power to enforce environmental and pollution laws against oil and gas drilling on federal lands, residents near those leases would have absorbed the pollution and health risks, taxpayers would have owed contract damages to companies whose leases were suspended, and plaintiffs (including indigent ones backed by third parties) could have been billed the drillers' attorney fees for losing environmental challenges.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have overridden state environmental and pollution control laws for drilling on federal lands, including laws that existing federal statutes expressly apply to such activity, removing a layer of protection communities near those lands currently have.

It would have limited the National Environmental Policy Act review for a federal or offshore oil and gas lease to a single statement and single review at the lessee's request, and barred any other federal agency from conducting its own review.

It would have defined 'significantly damage' so that destroying up to 5 percent of wildlife, fish, or marine or coastal environment in the lease area would not count as significant damage, and made suspensions beyond 90 days a contract breach the government would have to pay for.

It would have required losing appellants, including indigent parties and the third parties who helped fund them, to pay the drillers' attorney and witness fees and court costs, and defaulted appeals to the lessee if the Secretary or the D.C. Court of Appeals missed a deadline.

Supporters argued at the time that overlapping federal and state reviews and lease suspensions delayed energy production on federal land; the honest cost of their approach was weaker pollution control, a narrower definition of environmental harm, and new financial penalties on citizens who challenged drilling.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits would have flowed almost entirely to companies holding federal oil and gas leases, in the form of preemption of state law, faster permits, harder-to-suspend leases, and damages paid by taxpayers. The costs would have fallen on states that lost their regulatory authority, on residents near federal and offshore drilling who would have faced pollution with fewer legal remedies, and on citizens and advocacy groups who risked paying the industry's legal fees for losing a challenge. The bill contained no provisions directly benefiting ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees in September 2008, never got a hearing or a vote in either one, and died when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 10, 2008 and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee.
Fifteen days later it was assigned to the Natural Resources subcommittees on National Parks, Forests and Public Lands and on Energy and Mineral Resources, where it stayed.
No committee ever voted on the bill and the full House never voted on it; the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 and the bill died with it.
The bill's 18 cosponsors were all Republicans; there is no record of any Democratic support or of any vote ever being scheduled.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State environmental regulators and people who live near federal and offshore drilling leases are better off because the bill died, since state pollution laws and full federal environmental review would have kept applying. Oil and gas companies are not better off; they gained nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States and communities near drilling leases

for.name: Marsha Blackburn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which would have exempted federal-land oil and gas drilling from state environmental laws and limited federal environmental review.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.role: House Natural Resources Committee (Democratic majority, 110th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or a vote; it sat in subcommittee until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Oversight and Government Reform Committee
against.role: House Oversight and Government Reform Committee (Democratic majority, 110th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never took it up; the House never voted on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's sponsor and all 18 cosponsors were Republicans, with no recorded Democratic support.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies leasing federal and offshore lands
industries.note: The bill would have handed lessees preemption of state environmental rules, a 60-day permit deadline, near-irreversible leases, and taxpayer-paid damages if leases were suspended. Its gains come directly at the cost of the environmental oversight that applies to everyone else.

The bill would have restricted who can sue under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, forced environmental challengers to pay the drillers' legal fees if they lost, and routed all appeals through one court with deadlines that defaulted to the lessee. This would have made legal challenges to drilling far riskier and costlier.

industries.industry: State governments (environmental and pollution control agencies)
industries.note: The bill would have barred state environmental and pollution control laws from applying to any drilling activity under a federal lease, including laws that current federal law makes expressly applicable, and would have stripped state references from federal land planning statutes.
